summary:
Earth Jukebox is a sonification tool that translates Earth satellite images into real-time, spatial soundscapes. While NASA captures extraordinary visual data of our changing planet, relying solely on sight excludes blind and low-vision communities from images that only sighted people have been able to experience thus far

Our application solves this by scanning visual frames from left to right and classifying every pixel into five distinct physical Earth surface categories—deep water, shallow water, vegetation, bare ground/sand, and cloud cover. Each surface type is mapped to distinct organic timbres, stereo panning (left-to-right ear movement), vertical pitch mapping, and region-width sustain durations. By pairing real-time audio with a live side-by-side classified visual map ("What the Program Hears"), Earth Jukebox makes NASA Earth science intuitive, verifiable, and accessible to everyone. it is also scalable, meaning it can be changed to classify more than just five categories, and can use more than just a synthesizer for its instrument.
details: Earth Jukebox is an interactive, browser-based sonification application that transforms NASA Earth satellite imagery into real-time, spatial soundscapes. Rather than translating raw RGB values into arbitrary electronic beeps, our algorithm analyzes every pixel's hue, colorfulness, and brightness to classify visual frames into five physical Earth surface categories: deep water, shallow water, vegetation, bare ground/sand, and cloud cover. As the jukebox scans an image from left to right, horizontal position maps to stereo panning (moving smoothly from the listener's left ear to right ear), vertical height controls musical pitch (higher in the frame produces a higher note), and the horizontal width of each continuous terrain region determines how long its tone sustains. To make the experience both scientifically transparent and accessible, the interface pairs the original satellite frame side-by-side with a live "What the Program Hears" classified map, pixel-level readouts, and surface-area percentages. Users can explore curated NASA presets, switch between sound modes (such as surface instruments or deep continuous hums), drag-and-drop or paste (Ctrl+V) their own images, and navigate entirely via keyboard shortcuts (Space to play/stop, Left/Right arrows to switch tracks) to support blind and low-vision exploration. Designed with scalability in mind, the modular classification engine can easily expand beyond five surface categories, swap in new acoustic instruments, or process multi-frame climate time-lapses. By turning visual Earth science into an intuitive auditory experience, Earth Jukebox removes visual barriers for blind and low-vision communities while offering students, educators, and researchers a multi-sensory way to perceive planetary patterns. We built the application using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and the Web Audio API for low-latency browser synthesis and stereo panning, alongside Python image-processing prototypes. In accordance with Space Apps guidelines, Super Intelligence (SI) tools (Claude and Gemini) were utilized during development to assist with code prototyping, debugging, audio synthesis logic, and drafting presentation and submission text, while all system architecture, surface-mapping rules, and final integration were directed and verified by our team.
